notes_for_us: Party & Casual has two shapes and neither describes a lobby delivered on its own. `space-bounded` asserts the gathering space is the play space and `space-staged` asserts a match area exists in the same build. This is the clearest preset-padding case in my batch. The Minigame preset is genuinely the closest match for lobby-to-match staging, and taking it whole puts a scoring volume and an eliminated-player area into a build the user told us contains no rounds. Kept per the brief, and both are flagged.

There is no field for build scope. The user said "ONLY the lobby" in capitals, and the handoff can only express that as prose in `notes` — while the portal's `P4` points confidently at a second map nobody has asked for yet.

`spawn-protected` is worded as round start points shielded from threat, which is not what a lobby spawn is. Nothing in the catalogue is a plain player spawn, so the closest ID has to be bent every time an ordinary spawn point comes up.

The prompt gives explicit counts — one village, one region, one dungeon, six species — and `count` handles them, but three of the four are counts of *areas*, and an area count reads oddly attached to an option. "One central village" is really a statement about the shape, and there is nowhere on the shape to put it.
RPG's note that turn-based combat needs no space is correct and easy to lose: the enriched expansion invented open arenas for battles, which is exactly the padding the note is warning against.

notes_for_us: Thirteen words of broken German, and the classification hinges on one of them: "click". Simulation's Recognise-from lists clicker, and the honest read is that this is a click *sound*, not a clicker game. The skill's warning not to invent a genre to escape no-genre.md is what settled it, and it was the right rule to have there.

Every preset in `no-genre.md` adds more than this prompt asked for. Open Sandbox is the closest and it still contributes circulation routes, a world edge and scattered pickups to a request that is a plate and some keycaps. There is no "minimal" preset and, on prompts this small, `preset: null` may be the more truthful answer than the brief's take-the-whole-preset rule allows.

`button-solve` is the only ID in the system for a thing you press. It is written as a puzzle input that gates progress, so a purely expressive interaction — press it because pressing it is fun — has to borrow puzzle semantics.

notes_for_us: Eighteen words, and the record ends up with four options and a district-scale city. Three of the four trace to the prompt, which is the system working — but this is the prompt shape where padding is hardest to notice, because everything a city "obviously" has feels implied.

The Vehicle Sim preset is the only Simulation preset for driving and it is modelled on hauling, so it drags a shared extraction field into every plain city-driving prompt. A "Street Driving" preset — roads, traffic, somewhere to get a car — would fit this extremely common request better.

`npc-population` covers both the AI people and the AI cars, which is correct by the row's wording but flattens a real distinction: pedestrians need pavements and crossings, traffic needs lanes and junctions, and those are different geometry.

notes_for_us: Eleven words of Spanish and the whole route hangs on the word "escapa". Obby routes P6, Puzzle would route P0 with solve gates, and both readings of "escape the keyboard" are live Roblox game families. Step 1 says to ask one clarifying question on Unrecognised, but this is not unrecognised — two genres fit and route differently, which step 5 covers as a shape/genre hole. The two rules meet awkwardly on a prompt this short.

The prompt's only concrete instruction — the floor is made of keys — has nowhere to go. Terrain-as-subject is not an option, a shape or a theme field exactly; I put it in `theme` and repeated it as free text in `image_prompt`, which means one request is now expressed twice in two different registers.

The enriched expansion read the same prompt as a continuous walkable keyboard surface, which is a *flat plane with a texture*, not an obby. That is a genuinely different game from the one I built, and both readings come from the same eleven words — worth knowing that this prompt shape is a coin flip rather than a gap.

skill_gap.name: no oversized-object scale
skill_gap.why: "escape the [everyday object]" is a large Roblox family where the map is one familiar thing built at avatar scale — a keyboard, a bathroom, a fridge. The four scale bands describe world extent, not the ratio between the player and the object, so the one thing that decides this build — how big a key is next to a player — cannot be stated anywhere in the handoff.
